title: Sounds: listen up!
subtitle: creak, sizzle, deafening, peace and quiet
summary: Name noises exactly - doors creak, sausages sizzle, sirens wail - and describe silence with words like eerie, inaudible and as quiet as a mouse.

lesson.heading: Four words for a lack of sound
rows: silent
without noise, or not talking; used of people and things
They asked him several questions but he remained silent. / The house was completely silent. / silent films, made before sound was introduced
quiet
without much noise or activity, or not talking much
It's very quiet here at night. / I had a quiet day at work. / My dad was a quiet man.
noiseless(ly)
without noise; usually an adverb, formal or literary
He closed the door noiselessly behind him.
soundless(ly)
without sound; usually an adverb, formal or literary, for an unexpected lack of sound
The object vanished soundlessly into the night sky.
lesson.note: Noiseless and soundless are mostly used as adverbs and suggest that we would normally have expected to hear something.

lesson.heading: Verbs for specific noises: doors, wheels and walls
lesson.text: Each noise verb goes with its own typical nouns. A door **slams** (closes with a loud bang) or **creaks** (the noise of friction of wood or metal); a wheel or a hinge **squeaks** (a high, irritating noise); loud music **pounds** through a wall (a dull, beating sound); someone **hammers** at a door, knocking very loudly and repeatedly.

examples.text: The door **slammed** in the strong wind.
The old wooden door **creaked** as I opened it.
My bike wheel is **squeaking**. I need to get some oil.
We could hear our neighbours' favourite rock music **pounding** through the walls.
She **hammered** at the door but nobody answered.

lesson.heading: Verbs for specific noises: pans, guns, waves and horns
lesson.text: Food **sizzles** in a frying pan - that is the sound of frying. A shot **rings out**, a phrase used above all for gunfire. Waves **crash** on a beach, a loud, heavy noise. A car horn **hoots** or **toots**, and a siren **wails**, making a rising and falling sound.

examples.text: The sausages **sizzled** in the frying pan and smelt delicious.
A shot **rang out** and the bird fell from the sky.
From our cottage, we could hear the waves **crashing** on the beach below.
He always **hoots**/**toots** his horn to let us know he's arrived.
I could hear police car sirens **wailing** all last night.

lesson.heading: Adjectives for noise and silence
rows: eerie
strange and rather scary (an eerie silence)
deafening
extremely and painfully loud
grating
unpleasant and irritating (a grating voice)
piercing
high enough to hurt the ears (a piercing scream)
high-pitched
higher than most voices, like a whistle
inaudible
impossible to hear; faint is almost inaudible

lesson.heading: The adjectives at work
lesson.text: Notice which noun each adjective prefers. A silence is **eerie**; engines and music are **deafening**; a voice is **grating** or **high-pitched**; a scream is **piercing**; a recording or a whisper is **faint** or **inaudible**.

examples.text: There was an **eerie** silence in the old church.
The noise of the aircraft engines was **deafening**.
He has one of those **grating** voices that gets on my nerves.
She let out a **piercing** scream and fled as fast as she could.

lesson.heading: Fixed expressions about noise and silence
lesson.text: Four everyday phrases you will hear constantly. **You could have heard a pin drop** describes total silence, usually after a shock. **I can't hear myself think!** complains about too much noise. **Peace and quiet** is the calm period you long for after a noisy time, and someone **as quiet as a mouse** makes no sound at all.

examples.text: Everyone was so shocked and silent, **you could have heard a pin drop**.
Hey, you kids! Be quiet! **I can't hear myself think!**
I need **peace and quiet** after a busy day at work.
You're **as quiet as a mouse**! I didn't hear you come in at all.

lesson.text: Learn a noise verb together with the thing that makes it: doors **creak** and **slam**, hinges **squeak**, bacon **sizzles**, shots **ring out**, sirens **wail**, waves **crash**.

exercises.prompt: This luxury car prides itself on its almost ___ engine.
exercises.explanation: Noiseless means with no noise at all - here it is used as an adjective before engine.

exercises.prompt: It's very difficult to find a ___ place to live nowadays, even in the countryside.
exercises.explanation: Quiet describes a place without much noise or activity.

exercises.prompt: Charlie Chaplin's ___ films are as funny today as they were in the 1920s.
exercises.explanation: Silent films are films made before sound was introduced.

exercises.prompt: The great bird flapped its wings and rose ___ into the evening sky.
exercises.hint: (an adverb, for an unexpected lack of sound)
exercises.explanation: Soundlessly is used, often literarily, where we would normally expect to hear something - here, the wings.

exercises.prompt: The women kept up a ___ protest in front of the laboratories.
exercises.explanation: A silent protest is one made without talking or shouting.

exercises.prompt: Suddenly, a shot ___ out. Somebody was firing at the birds on the lake.
exercises.explanation: A shot rings out - the verb ring out is typically used for the sound of a gunshot.

exercises.prompt: The chicken ___ in the frying pan. The sound and the smell made me even more hungry.
exercises.explanation: Sizzle is the sound made by food frying.

exercises.prompt: We heard police sirens ___. There must have been an accident, or perhaps a robbery.
exercises.explanation: Sirens wail - they make a rising and falling sound.

exercises.prompt: The door ___. It was very old, made of oak and difficult to open.
exercises.explanation: Creak is the noise of friction of wood and/or metal; slam means to close with a loud bang.

exercises.prompt: The music was ___ through the walls. It was as if the musicians were playing in our bedroom.
exercises.explanation: Pounding is a dull, beating sound, typical of loud music through a wall.

exercises.prompt: The rusty door hinges are ___. I think they need some oil.
exercises.explanation: A squeak is a high, irritating noise, made by something that needs oil.

exercises.prompt: She ___ her horn. I looked out of the window and saw her car parked outside.
exercises.explanation: A car horn hoots or toots.

exercises.prompt: Match each description with the right adjective.

pairs.left: an extremely loud noise, e.g. very loud music
a high noise that hurts your ears
a harsh, irritating kind of voice
a voice with a tone like a whistle
a whisper that is almost impossible to hear

exercises.prompt: It was so quiet you could have heard a ___ drop.
exercises.explanation: You could have heard a pin drop means there was total silence.

exercises.prompt: I've had some noisy, hectic days with all those kids; now I'm looking forward to some peace and ___.
exercises.hint: (a calm period after a noisy time)
exercises.explanation: Peace and quiet is a calm, quiet period after a noisy time.

exercises.prompt: I don't even notice that Will is in the flat sometimes. He's as quiet as a ___.
exercises.explanation: As quiet as a mouse means very quiet indeed.

exercises.statement: If you say 'Turn that music down! I can't hear myself think!', you are complaining that there is too much noise.
exercises.explanation: Correct - I can't hear myself think! is said when people are making too much noise.

exercises.prompt: Is each word about noise or about silence?
